solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Continues the book, dismissing detective's first motive

indicators.note: to dismiss someone is to send them out of the room

parts.note: to read on is to continue a book
first letter of detective, taken out of READS ON

explanation.surface: A reader keeps going with a whodunnit, still hunting for the killer's motive.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive and 'first' look like part of a crime-fiction sentence; together they only pick out the D to be removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the reason behind an act is its motive.

clue.text: Ecstatic, intoxicated rich hosts upset party resort

indicators.note: a drunk person cannot keep things in order, so the letters of RICH stagger into a new arrangement
a host has guests inside the house
in a down clue, to upset something is to tip it over, so its letters read from the bottom up

explanation.surface: A wealthy, drunken host is thrilled to throw a party at a resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' covers both the party and the resort, not just the party, and in a down entry the tipped-over pair reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to be rhapsodic is to be carried away with enthusiasm, ecstatic.

clue.text: Very good set in a French city? Mostly

indicators.note: to set something in a frame is to place it inside
most but not all of the word is used, so NICE is cut before its final E

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a very fine place is a French city, half-sure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' does two jobs: it is the word for GEL, and 'set in' says where GEL goes.
explanation.definitionFit: By extension: angels are the model of goodness, so an angelic child is very good.

clue.text: Doctor Who is left looking wise

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, as with doctored figures, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The Doctor from Doctor Who is left looking thoughtful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor Who' is the famous BBC time-traveller, so the eye reads it as a name; here 'Doctor' is a verb acting on 'Who is' plus L.
explanation.definitionFit: The owl is the proverbial wise bird, so to look owlish is to look wise.

clue.text: Rabbit initially confused with Wonderland character

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the start of 'confused' is taken

parts.note: the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: The White Rabbit is getting muddled up with another Alice in Wonderland character.
explanation.walkthrough: Wonderland really has a White Rabbit, which is why the first word looks like a character too.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal: to rabbit (on) is to talk at length, to chatter.

clue.text: Philanthropy must do without it, displaying caution

indicators.note: to do without something is to go on having lost it

parts.note: the word itself, removed from CHARITY

explanation.surface: A cautious remark that philanthropy will have to manage without some funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' looks like a pronoun for the missing money; it is the literal letters to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: chary means wary, reluctant to take risks.

clue.text: Letters help to support Vaughan Williams, say, after overture lost

indicators.note: an overture is the opening of a piece, so losing it means the first letter goes
in a down clue a support sits underneath

parts.note: RALPH Vaughan Williams, the English composer, minus his first letter

explanation.surface: A letter writer offers help to the composer Vaughan Williams after one of his overtures went missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks Vaughan Williams as an example of a Ralph. Overture sounds musical, fitting the composer, but only means the R.
explanation.definitionFit: Collective sense: the alphabet is the full set of letters.

clue.text: Children's game and story incorporating new slogan

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take into the body

parts.note: a story is a fib, a lie

explanation.surface: A children's game and a story come bundled with a fresh advertising slogan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Story' sounds like a bedtime tale to go with the game; it is the fib sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a tagline is a catchphrase attached to a brand or film.

clue.text: Rhubarb that chap dipped in drink

parts.note: rum is a drink, the outer piece

explanation.surface: A stick of rhubarb that some fellow has dunked in his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Most solvers know rheum only as the watery discharge from eyes; the botanical name is the less familiar sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanical name: Rheum is the genus to which rhubarb belongs.

clue.text: Incumbent to be not entirely long

indicators.note: not entirely means not the whole thing, so OCCUR is given without its end

parts.note: to occur is to be (found), as in 'the word occurs twice'; minus R
to long for is to pant for

explanation.surface: An office-holder-in-waiting whose term turns out to be not quite long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incumbent to be' reads as 'incumbent-elect'; in fact 'to be' is its own piece, OCCUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the incumbent of a post is the one currently holding, or occupying, it.

clue.text: Everybody welcoming energy in star

explanation.surface: Everyone is making a star feel welcome and energetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' looks like a celebrity being welcomed; it is a real star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Proper name: Algol is a bright variable star in Perseus, the 'demon star'.

clue.text: Winner with time to swallow new celebratory drink?

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A winner takes time to gulp down a fresh drink to celebrate.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface describes the podium ritual, so the definition sits inside its own scene.
explanation.definitionFit: By association: champagne is the drink traditionally opened to celebrate.

clue.text: Speak about Irish city, but not northern city

indicators.note: N stands for northern, so 'not northern' strikes an N out

parts.note: to say is to speak, the outer piece
LISBURN, a city in Northern Ireland, minus N

explanation.surface: Someone talks about an Irish city but insists it is not a northern one.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that Lisburn is in Northern Ireland; 'not northern' only drops its final N. Salisbury is a cathedral city in Wiltshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Proper name: Salisbury is an English cathedral city.

clue.text: Universal principle? Nothing in principle abandoned by leader

indicators.note: a word abandoned by its leader has lost its first letter, so MAXIM drops the M

parts.note: a maxim is a principle; minus M

explanation.surface: A universal principle is questioned: a party leader has given up on principle entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principle' is written twice, once in the definition and once as MAXIM. 'Leader' reads as a politician; it is the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: an axiom is a principle accepted as universally true.

clue.text: Wharf where criminals are often seen?

definitions.meaning: first definition: a berth where ships load and unload
second definition: the enclosure in a courtroom where the accused stands

explanation.surface: A quay where villains are often spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: The docks sound like a crooks' hangout; the second sense is the dock in a courtroom, where the accused stands.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a dock is a wharf for ships, and the courtroom dock is the enclosure for the accused.

clue.text: Chap leading representative to secure me for the board?

indicators.note: whoever leads goes in front
to secure something is to hold it fast

explanation.surface: A man heading an agency hopes to get me appointed to the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secure me for the board' reads as a job appointment; 'secure' is the container, and 'for' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Collective sense: a company's board is its management.

clue.text: Comment on article, no thanks to editor first and foremost

indicators.note: foremost means at the very front, so only the front letter of each word counts

parts.note: first letters of to and editor

explanation.surface: A remark about an article, with no gratitude shown to the editor above all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ta' is everyday British for thank you. 'Article' looks like a newspaper piece to comment on; it is just AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to annotate a text is to add comments to it.

clue.text: Drunk grabbing a harmful bit of car

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold

explanation.surface: A drunk is snatching a dangerous part off a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' leads the clue like a noun, the person doing the grabbing; it is the adjective TIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Part for whole: a tail-light is the red lamp on the back of a car.

clue.text: Reduction in wharf rail transport — just a few lines here

indicators.note: a reduction makes something smaller, so QUAY is cut short by its last letter

explanation.surface: Cuts to trains serving the wharf leave only a few railway lines there.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'lines' look like railway track; they are lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic hint: a quatrain is a stanza of only four lines of verse.

clue.text: Advisor working with sovereign in court

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for court, the outer piece
a machine that is on is working
a sultan is a sovereign ruler

explanation.surface: An advisor works alongside the monarch at the royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal court fits the sovereign so well that 'court' reads as the scene rather than the abbreviation CT.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a consultant is a paid professional advisor.

clue.text: Subtle nude dancing around party in Pretoria

indicators.note: letters that dance move about, so NUDE is rearranged

parts.note: the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

explanation.surface: A discreet nude dance performed at a party in the South African capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Pretoria' just locates the party in South Africa; ANC is fixed in the middle while only NUDE moves.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: something nuanced shows fine shades of meaning, so it is subtle.

clue.text: Satirical writer approves a Kindle's content

indicators.note: the content of something is what it holds inside, so the answer lies within the words

explanation.surface: A satirist gives his blessing to the reading matter on a Kindle.
explanation.walkthrough: Saki was the pen name of H. H. Munro, writer of sharp satirical short stories. 'Content' looks like the Kindle's reading matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Pen name: Saki (H. H. Munro) was an Edwardian writer of satirical short stories.

clue.text: Complain about island accommodating heads of insurgent group

indicators.note: to accommodate guests is to house them

parts.note: Arran, an island off the west of Scotland, the outer piece

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so insurgent and group each give their first

parts.note: first letters of insurgent and group

explanation.surface: Complaints about an island that is sheltering rebel leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: The rebel group sounds like the target of the complaint, but it only supplies two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal sense: to arraign someone is to find fault with or accuse them.

clue.text: Paltry, exhibiting paltriness reduced by cunning

indicators.note: something reduced is made shorter, so MEAN loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Something paltry, made even more so by crafty trimming.
explanation.walkthrough: Mean here is the stingy sense, and 'paltriness' echoes the definition on purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: measly means contemptibly small, as in a measly tip.

clue.text: A lot of rubbish covering large item in garden

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so PANTS loses its last letter
a cover goes over and around

parts.note: PANTS, British slang for rubbish, minus S
L = large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A heap of rubbish is covering something big in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'pants' means rubbish or nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: By example: a plant is the typical thing growing in a garden.

clue.text: Italian food not to be found at the start of the dictionary?

parts.words: not to be found at the start
parts.note: beyond the start of the dictionary
A is the letter a dictionary begins with

explanation.surface: A remark that the Italian word for this food is not listed at the front of the dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: A word found after the A section is 'past A', which spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Category: pasta is the family of Italian dough foods, spaghetti and the rest.

clue.text: Church guy and doctor make better nurses

indicators.note: to nurse a baby is to hold it close

parts.note: to heal is to make better, the outer piece

explanation.surface: A churchman and a doctor improve the lot of nurses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' reads as the hospital staff that a doctor works with; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypernym: a cathedral is a bishop's principal church.

clue.text: Gang almost securing one million in heist?

definitions.note: the question mark marks a heist as one example of a crime

indicators.note: almost means nearly all, so CREW stops one letter short
to secure loot is to hold on to it

explanation.surface: A gang nearly bags a million in a robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as the heist itself; the question mark shows a heist is just one kind of crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a heist, a big robbery, is one kind of crime.

clue.text: Left-winger very much linked to US spy records?

parts.note: so = very much, as in 'so kind'

explanation.surface: A left-winger strongly tied to American intelligence files.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a leftist on the CIA's books is an unlikely picture; 'records' is a verb, LIST, not files.
explanation.definitionFit: Political sense: socialists sit on the left wing of politics.

clue.text: Perform like Ella Fitzgerald, enshrining women's jazz

indicators.note: to enshrine a relic is to enclose it in a shrine

parts.note: Ella Fitzgerald was a famous singer, the outer piece

explanation.surface: Singing in Ella Fitzgerald's style, keeping women's jazz alive.
explanation.walkthrough: Ella Fitzgerald sang swing, so the answer is right there in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyponym: swing is a style of big-band jazz.

clue.text: Piece of music with an opening for the flute at last

indicators.note: the opening of a word is where it starts, so 'the' gives its first letter
at last means at the very end, so 'flute' gives only its final letter

explanation.surface: A composition that finally gives the flute a chance to play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An opening for the flute' reads as a solo cue; 'an' is its own piece and 'the' is the word whose opening is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo term: an andante is a movement or piece played at a walking pace.

clue.text: Small bird, clearly grown and elegant, looking at the wings

indicators.note: the wings of a stage are its two sides, so each word gives its two ends

parts.note: first and last letters of clearly
first and last letters of grown
first and last letters of elegant

explanation.surface: A little bird, plainly grown and graceful, inspecting its wings.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the ugly duckling becoming a swan; 'wings' is the outer letters of each word.
explanation.definitionFit: By example: a cygnet is a young swan, a bird not yet full size.
